name: Trude Harms — Resident

choices: Press your hand flat against the east wall and measure the heat — then say aloud what you find.
Move to the cellar door and examine the orange light beneath it more closely before deciding anything.
Ask Lotte Voss directly what she touched and when, and whether she has told anyone else.
opening.narrative: It is shortly after one in the morning on 28 July 1943, and you have been in this cellar for ninety minutes. The single bulb died twenty minutes ago. Around you on the benches sit eleven neighbors — Wachter at the far end, Hanna Brandt with her children pressed against her side, Lotte Voss sitting very straight and very still, others you know by face and floor but not always by name. The raid has not sounded like the others. There were no individual explosions, no pattern of near and far — only a building roar that began perhaps forty minutes ago and has not varied since, as if the city above you has become a single continuous event. The brick at your shoulder is warm.

npcMoments.moment: Wachter says, into the dark, that the all-clear will come. That it always comes. That the rule exists because people who left cellars early in 1940 and 1941 died in the street.
Lotte Voss has not moved from the bench. Her hands are folded in her lap. She is looking at the strip of orange light under the door.

briefing: The bench slat presses into the back of your thighs and the brick at your shoulder is warm in a way that brick has no business being. You have been in this cellar or ones exactly like it perhaps forty times since the war began, and the wall has always been the coldest thing in the room — the cold that comes up from the earth through a meter of foundation masonry. Tonight it is warm, and it has been getting warmer for the last twenty minutes, and you have not said this aloud because you do not yet know what to do with it. Wachter is talking again, his slow deliberate voice filling the dark the way it always does, and he is right about the regulation — you know the regulation as well as he does. The strip of light under the door is the color of embers. Your mouth is against the damp rag you found in your coat pocket without quite deciding to reach for it, and each breath through it returns a little less than it should. You know where the canal is. You have walked to it every working morning for six years. One hundred meters north, up Wendenstrasse, and the water does not burn. The question is not whether you know what to do. The question is whether you are willing to be the one who does it, in the dark, against the word of every authority in this room, with eleven people watching to see if you are right.
description: You know this building and this neighborhood. You have no official authority, only four years of surviving raids by following the rules — and the specific, physical knowledge that something is wrong tonight that the rules do not account for.
perspective: Write in close second person from the perspective of a working-class Hamburg woman with practical intelligence and no official standing — someone whose authority, if she has any tonight, must be earned in the moment from people who have no reason to follow her.

failure.closing_line: You had the one thing that could have saved them, and you kept it politely to yourself.
failure.what_happened: You knew. Every nerve told you the stairwell was a flue and the coal chute was the way, and you said nothing — because Wachter had the authority and four years of obedience had worn the objection out of you. You waited for permission that the roaring air would never grant. When the stairwell finally came down in a sheet of orange, the cellar filled, and you crawled the wrong way, blind, until a hand you never saw shoved you through the coal chute and out. You lived on luck — someone else's hand, someone else's board kicked loose — while the room you'd stayed silent in became a grave. You reached the alley alone, on your knees, the knowledge already curdling in you.
failure.emotional_weight: The corrosive shame of the person who knew and stayed quiet — spared not by wisdom but by an accident of a hand in the dark, owing a life to strangers she failed.

partial.closing_line: You learned that being right isn't enough — you have to be right in time.
partial.what_happened: You argued with the wall and won too late. Wachter wanted order, the stairwell, the numbered exit, and you burned three minutes you didn't have proving the chute was passable — kicking the board, coughing, shouting names into smoke that swallowed them. When the group finally moved, the stairwell had already gone; you took them out low through the coal chute into the alley. Most made it to the canal. But old Frau Kessler behind you — heavy, slow, frightened of the black hole — you turned back for her and she was already gone, folded against the coal, and you had to choose the living over the dead and leave her. You reached the water with scorched hands and half the people you'd started with.
partial.emotional_weight: The arithmetic of a survivor: you saved who you could, and the ones you couldn't will sit at the foot of every stair for the rest of your life.

success.closing_line: The rules kept you alive for four years; the coal chute kept you alive for the fifth.
success.what_happened: You felt it before you understood it — the cellar door frame breathing, paint blistering along the coal chute, the air pulling toward the stairwell like a tide going out. Four years of Wachter's rules told you to stay put; the warmth in the wall told you the building above was already a chimney. You went to the coal chute you had loaded a thousand times, kicked out the loose board you'd noticed for months, and hauled the first neighbor through into the alley behind. You made them go low, wet their scarves at the burst standpipe, run the leeward gap between two collapsing tenements toward the canal. Eleven people out through a hole meant for coal. You came last, coat smoking, into a night the color of a forge.
success.emotional_weight: The quiet vindication of a person with no authority who was right, and the knowledge that knowing your own walls saved more lives than any rulebook.

character_hooks: I have my husband's last letter in my coat pocket — he wrote that his unit had no winter coats in December, and I have not trusted the system to provide what it promises since I read it.

I spent three years as a Selbstschutz volunteer on the fourth floor before my shift work made it impossible — I know where the sand buckets are on every landing, and I know the Durchbruch wall in the north corner of this cellar has never been tested.

Lotte Voss told me, just before the bulb died, that she had touched the east wall and it was already warm — she said it quietly, to me alone, and I have been sitting with that information for twenty minutes.
context_sentence: You are Trude Harms, a resident who knows this cellar, and the brick wall behind you is hot.
startingKnowledge: The Mittelkanal is approximately one hundred meters north up Wendenstrasse.
The brick wall at your back has never been warm in four years of raids.
The rule is to stay until the Entwarnung — and the rule has always been right before tonight.
